UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- More than one million people in Darfur are at risk of losing food, water and shelter in coming months, following the expulsion of international aid groups by Sudan's government, the United Nations' chief humanitarian coordinator said Tuesday. A Doctors without Borders medic helps a sick child in a Darfur refugee camp. The statement by coordinator John Holmes comes after a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation. The information was gathered from March 11-18 in hopes of stemming further troubles in Darfur after Sudan's government expelled 13 international relief organizations from the wartorn region. The announcement came on the same day that President Omar al-Bashir, now an indicted war criminal, ignored the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea. Also Tuesday, a Sudanese staffer working for a Canadian relief group was shot dead in Darfur. A full report of the assessment will be released soon, according to the U.N., but an executive summary and recommendations were made available on Tuesday. "While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] which are left, to plug some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are at the same time, 'Band-Aid' solutions, not long term solutions," Holmes said. The U.N. estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur are dependent on healthcare support, 1.1 million need regular food aid, and another 1 million are in need of clean drinking water. The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which is still allowed to operate in Sudan, is carrying out a one-time-only distribution program in March and April, but that new partners will be needed to continue delivering food after April. After the International Criminal Court charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity on March 4, Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the permits of three organizations in the country. Bashir -- the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the court -- has continued to say that humanitarian efforts in the country should be "Sudanized." "Within a year, we don't want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen," he said at a rally a week after his arrest warrant was issued. Holmes said that 13,000 to 14,000 aid workers in the region already were Sudanese nationals. Holmes said the cooperation and technical help from the Sudanese government on the assessment was a good step forward. But he called it "only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions." Sudan's U.N. Ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he has information implicating the ousted organizations in activities contrary to their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public. One claim is that some organizations acted as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes denied those allegations, saying they remain unfounded. "Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence," he said. "In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done." The British aid organization, Oxfam, one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, released a statement in response to Tuesday's findings. "Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time," the statement said. "As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death. "With the humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will be an enormous challenge for others to tackle," Oxfam said.

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — More than one million people in Darfur risk losing access to food, water, and shelter in the coming months following the Sudanese government’s expulsion of international aid groups, the United Nations’ chief humanitarian coordinator said Tuesday.

A Doctors Without Borders medic assists a sick child in a Darfur refugee camp.

The statement by U.N. humanitarian coordinator John Holmes followed a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation. Information was gathered from March 11 to 18 in an effort to prevent further deterioration in Darfur after Sudan’s government expelled 13 international relief organizations from the war-torn region.

The announcement came the same day that President Omar al-Bashir, now an indicted war criminal, defied the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea.

Also Tuesday, a Sudanese staff member working for a Canadian relief organization was shot dead in Darfur.

A full assessment report will be released soon, according to the U.N., but an executive summary and recommendations were made available Tuesday.

“While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] which are left, to plug some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are at the same time, ‘Band-Aid’ solutions, not long-term solutions,” Holmes said.

The U.N. estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur depend on healthcare support, 1.1 million require regular food aid, and another 1 million need clean drinking water.

The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which remains authorized to operate in Sudan, is carrying out a one-time-only distribution program in March and April, but new partners will be needed to continue delivering food after April.

After the International Criminal Court charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity on March 4, Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the permits of three organizations operating in the country.

Bashir — the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the court — has continued to insist that humanitarian efforts in the country should be “Sudanized.”

“Within a year, we don’t want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen,” he said at a rally one week after his arrest warrant was issued.

Holmes said that 13,000 to 14,000 aid workers in the region were already Sudanese nationals.

He added that the Sudanese government’s cooperation and technical assistance during the assessment marked a positive step forward. However, he described it as “only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions.”

Sudan’s U.N. ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he possesses information implicating the expelled organizations in activities contrary to their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public.

One allegation is that some organizations acted as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes denied those allegations, saying they remain unsubstantiated.

“Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence,” he said. “In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done.”

The British aid organization Oxfam, one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, released a statement in response to Tuesday’s findings.

“Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time,” the statement said. “As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death.

“With the humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will be an enormous challenge for others to tackle,” Oxfam said.

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — The United Nations’ top humanitarian official warned Tuesday that over a million people in Darfur could lose access to food, water and shelter in the months ahead after Sudan’s government forced international aid organizations out of the country.

In a Darfur refugee camp, a Doctors Without Borders medical worker assists an ill child.

John Holmes, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator, issued the warning after a joint review conducted by the United Nations and Sudanese officials. The assessment was carried out between March 11 and March 18, with the aim of preventing conditions in Darfur from worsening after Khartoum expelled 13 foreign relief agencies from the conflict-affected region.

The warning was made the same day Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir, who has been indicted as a war criminal, traveled to Eritrea despite the possibility of arrest. Also on Tuesday, a Sudanese employee of a Canadian aid organization was shot and killed in Darfur.

The U.N. said a complete version of the assessment would be published soon, while an executive summary and a set of recommendations were released Tuesday.

Holmes said the Sudanese government, the United Nations and the nongovernmental organizations still operating in the area were working hard to cover some urgent shortages. However, he described those efforts as temporary fixes rather than lasting answers.

According to U.N. figures, 1.5 million people in Darfur rely on healthcare assistance, 1.1 million require routine food support, and another 1 million need safe drinking water.

The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which remains permitted to work in Sudan, is conducting a one-time food distribution effort during March and April. It added that additional partners will be necessary if food deliveries are to continue beyond April.

On March 4, after the International Criminal Court accused Bashir of war crimes and crimes against humanity, the Sudanese government expelled 13 international aid groups and canceled the operating permits of three organizations in the country.

Bashir, the first sitting national leader to be charged with war crimes by the court, has continued to argue that humanitarian work in Sudan should be “Sudanized.”

Speaking at a rally one week after the arrest warrant against him was issued, Bashir said that within a year he did not want any foreign aid organization working directly with Sudanese citizens.

Holmes noted that between 13,000 and 14,000 aid workers already operating in the region were Sudanese nationals.

He said Sudan’s cooperation and technical assistance during the assessment represented a positive initial move. Still, he said it was “only the first of many steps” needed to prevent the people of Darfur from facing serious harm as a result of the expulsions.

Sudan’s ambassador to the United Nations, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly claimed he possesses information showing that the expelled groups engaged in activities inconsistent with their humanitarian roles. He has not publicly released any such information.

One allegation is that some of the organizations served as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes rejected those accusations, saying they had not been substantiated.

He said that although Sudanese officials had referred to files containing evidence, the United Nations had not received any of it. Without that evidence, he said, no serious investigation could take place.

Oxfam, the British aid group and one of the organizations ordered out of Sudan, issued a statement in response to Tuesday’s findings.

The organization said the current emergency measures would work only briefly. It warned that when the rainy season begins within the next two months, people staying in fragile temporary shelters in areas vulnerable to flooding—where latrines may fill up and overflow—will face a severe danger of illness and death.

Oxfam added that because humanitarian capacity has been cut by almost half, other groups will face a major challenge in responding to such emergencies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about the U.N. warning that over one million people in Darfur could lose access to food, water, and shelter after Sudan expelled international aid groups following the ICC warrant for Omar al-Bashir.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N.: More than 1 million in Darfur at risk after Sudan expels aid groups**

**KHARTOUM, Sudan** — More than one million people in Sudan’s Darfur region could soon be cut off from critical supplies of food, clean water and shelter after the government expelled several international aid organizations, the United Nations warned.

The expulsions came after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir, accusing him of war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with the conflict in Darfur. Sudan has rejected the warrant and accused aid groups of cooperating with the court, allegations the organizations deny.

U.N. officials said the removal of major relief agencies threatens to deepen an already severe humanitarian crisis in Darfur, where years of fighting have displaced millions of people and left large portions of the population dependent on outside assistance.

Aid groups ordered to leave had been providing essential services in camps and remote communities, including food distribution, water sanitation, health care and emergency shelter. Without them, humanitarian workers warn, disease and malnutrition could spread quickly, especially among children and displaced families.

The United Nations said it was urgently assessing how to fill the gaps, but officials cautioned that replacing the expelled organizations would not be easy. Many had operated in Darfur for years and had staff, equipment and local networks already in place.

Humanitarian agencies have called on Sudan to reverse the decision, saying civilians should not be punished for political disputes. International leaders also expressed concern that the expulsions could violate Sudan’s obligation to allow humanitarian access to vulnerable populations.

The ICC warrant marked the first time the court sought the arrest of a sitting head of state. Prosecutors allege al-Bashir bears responsibility for atrocities committed during Sudan’s campaign against rebel groups in Darfur. Sudan’s government denies targeting civilians and says the court’s action is politically motivated.

The Darfur conflict began in 2003 when rebel groups took up arms, accusing the government of neglecting the region. The fighting prompted a brutal counterinsurgency campaign and a massive displacement crisis. International estimates say hundreds of thousands have died from violence, disease and hunger, though Sudan disputes those figures.

U.N. officials warned that unless aid operations resume quickly, the consequences could be immediate and severe.

“This is not about politics,” one humanitarian official said. “It is about whether families have food to eat, water to drink and a roof over their heads.”

counterfactuals.output:
**UNITED NATIONS, March 5, 2009** — The United Nations warned Thursday that Sudan’s expulsion of 13 foreign aid organizations from Darfur could trigger a major humanitarian crisis, cutting off food, water, medical care and shelter for hundreds of thousands of civilians already dependent on outside assistance.

Sudan ordered the groups to leave after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Omar Hassan al-Bashir on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur. Khartoum accused the organizations of cooperating with the court, an allegation the aid agencies rejected.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, said the expulsions would have “a very serious impact” on relief operations in Darfur and other parts of Sudan.

“The government has taken a decision which, if implemented fully, would have a major humanitarian impact,” Holmes told reporters at U.N. headquarters. He said the affected organizations made up a large share of the relief effort in Darfur, where millions of people have been displaced by years of conflict.

Holmes said the expelled agencies were responsible for substantial portions of health care, water and sanitation, nutrition programs and shelter support. He warned that replacing them quickly would be extremely difficult.

“These organizations are key partners in the humanitarian operation,” he said. “You cannot simply remove that capacity overnight without consequences for the people who depend on it.”

According to U.N. officials, roughly 4.7 million people in Darfur receive some form of humanitarian assistance, including more than 2.7 million people displaced from their homes. The removal of major international relief groups threatens to disrupt services in camps across the region, where civilians rely on aid agencies for clean water, medical clinics, food distribution and protection programs.

Among the organizations ordered out were Oxfam, CARE, Save the Children, the International Rescue Committee, Médecins Sans Frontières sections, and other major relief agencies. Sudan also moved against several local organizations.

Oxfam reacted with alarm, saying the decision would put vulnerable civilians at risk and undermine one of the world’s largest humanitarian operations.

“We are deeply concerned for the hundreds of thousands of people who rely on our work for clean water, sanitation and public health support,” Oxfam said in response to the Sudanese order. The agency said it had worked in Sudan for decades and denied any involvement with the International Criminal Court.

Oxfam officials said the expulsion would immediately affect communities in Darfur that depend on its water and sanitation programs, including displaced families living in crowded camps.

Humanitarian officials said the timing of the expulsions was especially dangerous because aid operations in Darfur require extensive logistics, security arrangements and experienced staff. Many programs are delivered in remote areas where government capacity is limited and insecurity remains high.

Holmes said the United Nations was seeking urgent clarification from Sudanese authorities and pressing Khartoum to reverse or soften the decision. He stressed that humanitarian agencies must be allowed to operate independently and impartially.

“Our concern is not political,” Holmes said. “Our concern is for the welfare of the people of Darfur and elsewhere in Sudan who need assistance.”

The Sudanese government has insisted that national organizations and remaining agencies can fill the gap. But U.N. officials and aid groups said the scale of the expulsions makes that unlikely in the short term.

The crisis follows the ICC’s decision to issue a warrant for Bashir, the first sitting head of state indicted by the court. The charges stem from the conflict in Darfur, which erupted in 2003 when rebel groups took up arms against the Sudanese government, accusing it of marginalizing the region. Khartoum responded with a military campaign and allied militia forces, leading to mass displacement and widespread atrocities.

The United Nations says the conflict has left hundreds of thousands dead and driven millions from their homes. Sudan disputes the death toll.

U.N. officials said they would continue talks with Khartoum while assessing which life-saving programs were most at risk. Relief agencies warned that any prolonged interruption could quickly worsen conditions in camps and rural communities.

“The people who will suffer from this are ordinary civilians,” one humanitarian official said. “They have already lost their homes, their livelihoods and their security. Now they risk losing the assistance that keeps them alive.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an article summarizing the March 2009 Darfur aid crisis: Sudan’s expulsion of NGOs, Bashir’s war crimes indictment, U.N. assessment findings, and risks to food, healthcare, and clean water access.
counterfactuals.output:
## Darfur Aid Crisis Deepens After Sudan Expels Relief Groups

In March 2009, Sudan’s already fragile humanitarian situation in Darfur was thrown into crisis after the government expelled major international aid organizations in response to the International Criminal Court’s decision to issue an arrest warrant for President Omar Hassan al-Bashir.

The ICC warrant, announced on March 4, 2009, accused Bashir of war crimes and crimes against humanity connected to Sudan’s counterinsurgency campaign in Darfur. Prosecutors alleged that Sudanese government forces and allied Janjaweed militias had carried out murder, rape, forced displacement, and attacks on civilians. The court did not initially include genocide charges in the warrant, though those allegations remained central to international debate over Darfur.

Khartoum rejected the ICC’s action as politically motivated and retaliated almost immediately by ordering the expulsion of 13 international nongovernmental organizations and closing several Sudanese aid groups. Among the organizations affected were some of the largest providers of humanitarian assistance in Darfur, including groups involved in food distribution, medical care, water and sanitation, and shelter support. The Sudanese government accused the NGOs of cooperating with the ICC, an allegation the aid agencies denied.

The expulsions alarmed the United Nations and humanitarian officials because Darfur’s civilian population was heavily dependent on outside aid. Years of conflict had displaced millions of people, many of whom were living in camps with limited access to farmland, markets, clinics, and safe water. The removal of experienced relief groups threatened to disrupt services that had been built up over years.

A U.N.-led assessment conducted after the expulsions found that the immediate collapse of aid operations had been partly avoided through emergency measures by U.N. agencies, remaining NGOs, and Sudanese authorities. However, the assessment warned that major gaps remained and that the situation could deteriorate quickly if capacity was not restored. The expelled organizations had been responsible for a significant share of essential services, and replacing their staff, supply chains, equipment, and local knowledge would be difficult.

Food access was one of the most urgent concerns. Humanitarian agencies warned that more than one million people could be affected by disruptions to food distribution and nutrition programs. Even where food stocks existed, the loss of logistics networks and field staff risked delays in delivery, especially in remote or insecure areas. Children, pregnant women, and displaced families were particularly vulnerable to malnutrition if regular assistance broke down.

Healthcare services were also at risk. Expelled organizations had operated clinics, supported hospitals, provided vaccinations, treated injuries and infectious diseases, and assisted survivors of sexual violence. U.N. officials warned that hundreds of thousands of people could lose access to basic medical care. In crowded camps, interruptions in healthcare also increased the danger of disease outbreaks.

Clean water and sanitation posed another major threat. Many displaced communities depended on aid groups to maintain boreholes, pumps, water trucking, latrines, and hygiene programs. Without those services, access to safe drinking water could decline sharply, raising the risk of diarrheal disease and other waterborne illnesses. The onset of warmer weather and the approach of the rainy season added to fears that poor sanitation and contaminated water could trigger broader public health emergencies.

The March 2009 crisis highlighted the deep connection between political conflict and humanitarian survival in Darfur. Bashir’s indictment intensified Sudan’s confrontation with international institutions, while the expulsion of aid groups placed civilians at renewed risk. Although emergency efforts prevented an immediate catastrophe, U.N. findings made clear that Darfur’s displaced population remained dangerously dependent on sustained humanitarian access, and that restrictions on aid could quickly translate into shortages of food, healthcare, and clean water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Recreate a CNN breaking-news-style story about Sudan, Darfur refugees, expelled aid agencies, the World Food Programme’s temporary food distribution, and U.N. concerns about “Band-Aid” solutions.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS: U.N. warns temporary food aid for Darfur refugees is only a “Band-Aid” as crisis deepens**

**KHARTOUM, Sudan** — The United Nations is warning that emergency food distributions to people displaced by the Darfur conflict are only a short-term fix after Sudan expelled several major international aid organizations, leaving critical gaps in humanitarian assistance.

The World Food Programme has begun temporary food distributions aimed at reaching vulnerable communities affected by the expulsion of aid groups that had been providing food, medical care, clean water and shelter support to displaced families.

U.N. officials say the move is urgently needed but far from sufficient.

“This is a Band-Aid,” one U.N. humanitarian official said, warning that temporary distributions cannot replace the broad network of aid agencies that had been operating across Darfur and other parts of Sudan.

The expulsions followed an international arrest warrant for Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir on allegations linked to war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur. Sudan’s government accused some aid organizations of cooperating with the International Criminal Court, a charge the agencies denied.

Humanitarian groups say the expulsions have disrupted lifesaving services for millions of people, many of whom are living in camps after years of violence between government-backed forces, rebel groups and militias.

The World Food Programme says it is working to prevent immediate food shortages, but U.N. officials caution that food deliveries alone cannot meet the population’s needs. Health clinics, sanitation programs and child nutrition services have all been affected.

Aid workers fear that without a broader solution, displaced families could face rising hunger, disease outbreaks and worsening insecurity in the camps.

The United Nations is urging Sudan to allow humanitarian operations to resume at full scale, warning that the loss of experienced aid organizations could quickly turn an already fragile situation into a larger emergency.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed international news piece on the consequences of Sudan “Sudanizing” humanitarian aid in Darfur, mentioning the ICC charges against President Omar al-Bashir, John Holmes’ statements, and Oxfam’s warning about the rainy season.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sudan’s Push to “Sudanize” Aid in Darfur Raises Fears of Humanitarian Breakdown**

*By [Reporter Name]*

Sudan’s attempt to replace expelled international aid agencies with local organizations and government-managed relief operations in Darfur is drawing growing international concern, with U.N. officials and humanitarian groups warning that the policy risks leaving hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people without adequate food, clean water, medical care and sanitation.

The strategy, widely described by diplomats and aid workers as the “Sudanization” of humanitarian assistance, follows Khartoum’s decision to expel a number of major foreign aid organizations after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Omar al-Bashir. The ICC charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity over the conflict in Darfur, accusing him of responsibility for a campaign of murder, extermination, forcible transfer, torture and rape. Bashir has rejected the charges, denouncing the court as a tool of Western powers and insisting Sudan can manage relief needs without the expelled agencies.

But the consequences of that decision are now becoming increasingly visible across Darfur’s vast camps and remote rural areas, where millions have depended for years on international humanitarian operations.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, warned that Sudanese authorities and local organizations could not simply substitute for the capacity of the expelled groups overnight. He said the gaps created by their departure were real and significant, particularly in areas such as water supply, sanitation, health care and nutrition.

Holmes acknowledged that Sudanese officials had moved quickly to assign local bodies and government agencies to take over some work, but he cautioned that the replacement effort was not equivalent to the large-scale operations previously run by experienced international organizations. The expelled agencies had extensive logistics networks, specialist staff, vehicles, warehouses, communications systems and established relationships inside camps for displaced people. Losing that infrastructure, he suggested, could not be remedied by administrative decree.

The concern is especially acute because Darfur’s humanitarian system is not a peripheral service but a lifeline. Years of conflict among Sudanese government forces, allied militias and rebel movements have displaced millions of people. Many families in camps remain dependent on food distributions, water trucking, basic clinics and disease prevention programs. Aid officials say even short disruptions can have severe consequences in areas where malnutrition is already present and where public health systems are weak.

Oxfam has warned that the approaching rainy season could deepen the crisis. Heavy rains in Darfur regularly turn dirt roads into mud, isolate communities and complicate the delivery of supplies. The agency cautioned that if stockpiles, water systems and health services are not secured before the rains begin, humanitarian access could deteriorate sharply. Flooding and poor sanitation also raise the risk of waterborne disease, including diarrhea and cholera-like outbreaks, especially in crowded camps.

The rainy season is a recurring logistical challenge for aid agencies in Darfur, but this year the danger is magnified by the sudden reduction in experienced humanitarian capacity. Organizations that had previously pre-positioned supplies and maintained access routes are no longer operating in many areas. Their departure has left behind not only operational gaps but also uncertainty about monitoring: international aid workers often served as independent observers of conditions inside camps and rural communities.

Sudan’s government argues that foreign organizations had overstepped their humanitarian mandate and interfered in political affairs. Officials have said national groups can deliver aid more appropriately and with greater respect for Sudanese sovereignty. Khartoum also maintains that reports of a looming humanitarian disaster are exaggerated and politically motivated.

However, Western governments, U.N. agencies and international NGOs say the issue is not sovereignty but capacity. They argue that local organizations, while important, often lack the funding, equipment, technical expertise and freedom of movement needed to replace major international agencies at scale. Some Sudanese groups also face pressure from local authorities, raising questions about their ability to operate independently and to report needs honestly.

The expulsion of aid groups has also strained relations between Sudan and the United Nations at a moment when the country is already under intense diplomatic scrutiny. The ICC warrant against Bashir marked the first time the court sought the arrest of a sitting head of state. Khartoum’s response—expelling aid organizations it accused of cooperating with the court—has been widely interpreted as a message to international actors operating in Sudan.

For displaced Darfuris, the political confrontation has immediate practical consequences. Camp leaders and residents have reported worries over declining medical services, reduced water maintenance and uncertainty about food distribution schedules. Aid workers say programs most at risk include therapeutic feeding for malnourished children, maternal health care, vaccination support, hygiene promotion and maintenance of boreholes and pumps.

Humanitarian officials fear that the damage may become harder to reverse the longer the policy continues. Relief systems depend on continuity: supply chains must be maintained, staff must be paid, equipment repaired and disease surveillance sustained. If those systems falter during the rainy season, the result could be a cascade of worsening health, hunger and displacement.

Holmes has urged Sudan to allow humanitarian operations to be restored to the level needed to protect civilians, emphasizing that aid access must be based on needs rather than political disputes. While U.N. agencies remain in the country, many depend on nongovernmental partners to implement programs on the ground. Without those partners, the reach of the U.N. system is limited.

Oxfam’s warning underscores the urgency. Once rains cut off roads, delayed action may no longer be enough. Supplies that are not in place beforehand may not reach isolated areas for weeks or months. In a region where many communities are already living close to the edge, such delays can be deadly.

The broader fear among diplomats and humanitarian agencies is that “Sudanizing” aid could become less a transition to local ownership than a forced contraction of relief at the expense of civilians. While building Sudanese humanitarian capacity is widely viewed as a legitimate long-term goal, aid officials say it cannot happen through the abrupt removal of experienced agencies in the middle of an ongoing emergency.

As the standoff continues, Darfur’s displaced population remains caught between international justice, national sovereignty and humanitarian necessity. The ICC’s case against Bashir has intensified Sudan’s confrontation with the outside world, but the immediate burden is falling on families who have already endured years of war. For them, the test of Sudan’s new aid policy will not be political rhetoric, but whether water keeps flowing, clinics stay open and food arrives before the rains.
